title: Trump calls Georgia election official to interfere in county investigation
description_short: Trump calls Georgia election official to interfere in county investigation
description_medium: On December 23, 2020, President Donald Trump called Frances Watson, the Georgia elections investigator overseeing a review of Cobb County mail-ballot signatures. According to the supplied account, Trump told Watson she would be a hero if she found a way to turn Georgia red. Her office was then auditing more than 15,000 signatures. The call put direct presidential pressure on an official conducting an election inquiry.
description_long: Donald Trump called Frances Watson on December 23, 2020, while she was leading an investigation into allegations of ballot fraud in Georgia. Watson was overseeing an audit of more than 15,000 signatures on mail-in ballots in Cobb County. The supplied account says Trump told her that she would be a hero if she found a way to turn the state red. The call therefore concerned the outcome of a state whose certified presidential result he was challenging, and it targeted an investigator responsible for examining election material. The account describes what Trump said but does not establish that Watson changed her findings or that the audit uncovered fraud. Its significance lies in the president contacting an official involved in the review and urging a result favorable to him. The linked reporting includes audio of the conversation, providing a contemporaneous basis for the reported exchange. The episode illustrates pressure on election administration during the post-election dispute, while the available entry does not claim that the call altered Georgia’s count or the investigator’s work.

The reported risk was that attackers could have reached confidential court information, including sealed filings and other sensitive records. Such files can contain information with implications for national security, trade secrets, investigative work, whistleblowers, and arrest warrants. The supplied synopsis characterizes access to sealed documents as likely; it does not establish that every listed type of material was actually obtained, nor does it specify which individual files the attackers viewed or copied. The judiciary’s response was to investigate an apparent compromise of its case-management system, as described in the linked Reuters report. The breach raised a serious cybersecurity concern because court systems hold information that is not available to the public. This entry focuses on the disclosure and its potential exposure of sensitive material, not on a claim that the system’s entire archive was stolen or that a particular case was affected.

title: Trump: Alexandra Chalupa: Trump's next move is getting states to secede
description_short: Trump: Alexandra Chalupa: Trump's next move is getting states to secede
description_medium: In a January 2021 warning, Democratic operative Alexandra Chalupa said Trump allies could seek state secession and alleged Paul Manafort was involved. Her comments followed the January 6 attack on the Capitol and drew on fears about continued efforts to undermine the election. The supplied material presents this as Chalupa’s prediction and concern, not as proof that a secession plan existed.

She said the Trump family and allies might seek to encourage states to secede and alleged that Manafort was involved. Her warning came days after a mob attacked the U.S. Capitol while Congress met to certify the 2020 election. The supplied account also refers to federal warnings about possible local, state, and federal threats, but it does not give enough detail to attribute a specific government assessment. The available record supports documenting the warning and its context while keeping the underlying allegation attributed to Chalupa. title: Donald Trump starts brainstorming the Patriot Party, a GOP rival
description_short: Donald Trump starts brainstorming the Patriot Party, a GOP rival
description_medium: Between January 11 and 15, 2021, Donald Trump reportedly discussed with aides and allies forming a new political party, tentatively called the Patriot Party. The conversations followed his defeat in the 2020 election and the January 6 attack on the Capitol. The proposal would have challenged the Republican Party’s hold on his political supporters, but the supplied account does not say Trump formally organized or launched a party.
description_long: In the days after the January 6 attack on the U.S. Capitol, Donald Trump reportedly began discussing a new political party with aides and allies. The conversations took place sometime between January 11 and January 15, 2021, and the name under consideration was the Patriot Party. The idea emerged as Trump left office after losing the 2020 election and faced a second impeachment trial. A new party could have split Republican voters or created a separate vehicle for Trump’s political influence, but the supplied account documents brainstorming rather than a formal organization, filing, or launch. It also quotes a commentator who doubted Trump would do the sustained work required to build a party; that assessment is opinion rather than evidence about his intentions. Later reporting on Patriot Party supporter groups suggests the label circulated among Trump supporters, but it does not by itself show that Trump established a national party. This entry records the reported discussions and the political context without treating a proposal as a completed organization.

title: Trump: 45 Senate Republicans vote to make impeaching Donald Trump illegal
description_short: Trump: 45 Senate Republicans vote to make impeaching Donald Trump illegal
description_medium: On January 26, 2021, the Senate voted on Rand Paul’s point of order that trying a former president after leaving office was unconstitutional. Forty-five Republican senators supported the motion, while the chamber rejected it, allowing Donald Trump’s second impeachment trial to proceed. The vote came shortly after senators were sworn in as jurors and previewed a central constitutional argument in the trial.
description_long: The Senate considered whether it could constitutionally try Donald Trump after he had left the presidency. On January 26, 2021, Kentucky Republican Rand Paul raised a point of order arguing that the impeachment trial was invalid because Trump was no longer in office. The Senate voted on Paul’s motion shortly after senators had been sworn in as jurors for the second impeachment trial. Forty-five Republican senators voted in support of the point of order, but the motion failed, so the trial continued. The vote showed that a substantial bloc of Republicans backed a jurisdictional objection, while the chamber as a whole declined to end the proceedings on that basis. It did not make impeachment of former officials illegal: the Senate rejected the motion, and the trial went forward. The question of trying a former president became a central constitutional issue in the proceedings. This account describes the procedural vote and its immediate effect without conflating the motion with the later verdict or claiming that the Senate adopted Paul’s position.

title: Trump: Mitch McConnell tells Republicans he won't vote to convict Trump
description_short: Trump: Mitch McConnell tells Republicans he won't vote to convict Trump
description_medium: Ahead of the Senate’s second impeachment verdict on February 13, 2021, Minority Leader Mitch McConnell told Republican colleagues he would vote to acquit Donald Trump. McConnell argued that Trump could not be convicted after leaving office, even as he later condemned Trump’s role in the January 6 attack. The announcement signaled that conviction would fall short of the two-thirds threshold.
description_long: On February 13, 2021, during the fifth day of Donald Trump’s second impeachment trial, Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell informed Republican senators that he planned to vote to acquit. According to the supplied account and linked NBC reporting, McConnell said he believed the Senate could not convict Trump because Trump had already left office. The statement came before the final vote and helped make clear that the Senate would not reach the two-thirds majority required for conviction. McConnell’s position did not mean he endorsed Trump’s conduct: after the acquittal vote, he publicly blamed Trump for provoking the January 6 attack while maintaining that the Senate lacked jurisdiction once Trump’s term ended. The distinction between his constitutional argument and his assessment of Trump’s conduct is important to understanding the episode. The record documents his advance notice to colleagues and his stated reason for acquittal; it does not treat the argument as a settled constitutional rule or imply that the trial was halted.

title: Trump Admin censors health officials & ends lifesaving HIV program
description_short: Trump Admin censors health officials & ends lifesaving HIV program
description_medium: In late January 2025, the Trump administration directed international health organizations to stop using U.S.-funded HIV medicines, including supplies already delivered to local clinics, then shut down data systems for the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief. These steps disrupted a major foreign-aid program and limited access to its information. The supplied account does not quantify treatment interruptions or deaths.
description_long: In late January 2025, the Trump administration issued instructions affecting the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief, or PEPFAR, the U.S.-funded program supporting HIV treatment abroad. International health organizations were told to stop using HIV medicines purchased with American aid, even when supplies had already reached local clinics. At 6 p.m. Eastern, the administration also shut down PEPFAR data systems, according to the supplied account. The actions put both ongoing treatment and the program’s ability to access information at issue. The record does not quantify how many clinics stopped dispensing medication, how many patients missed treatment, or how long the data systems remained unavailable. Reuters later reported that U.S. health agencies removed HIV-related and other data, providing related context for the information disruption. These are consequential operational changes to an established public-health program, but specific downstream health outcomes cannot be inferred from the available synopsis. This entry documents the instructions and system shutdown while leaving the scale of treatment effects and their duration unresolved.
